name: Kazinczy Street Orthodox Synagogue
description: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue is the great Orthodox synagogue of Pest's Jewish Quarter, built in 1912 and 1913 by the Löffler brothers in an Art Nouveau style influenced by Ödön Lechner. A Hebrew inscription crosses its brick facade, and the complex around it has included a school and a ritual bath.

children.text: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue stands in Erzsébetváros, in the heart of the old Jewish Quarter, and was built for the Orthodox Jewish community of Pest. In the late nineteenth century Pest's Jewish community had divided into three branches, the Neolog, the Status Quo Ante and the Orthodox. The congregation's own site gives the address as Kazinczy utca 29–31, as do the BKK listing and Wikipedia, while a few visitor sites give 27–29; the building itself dominates the narrow street.

The architects were the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. A competition was announced on 25 June 1909, and a jury favoured another design, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and chose the Löfflers' plans, which were approved in detail on 8 November 1910. The school and the community headquarters were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912, and in July 1913 the architects submitted a revised facade design, which Hungarian Wikipedia describes as plainer and cheaper, although English Wikipedia describes the change as making the main facade more ornate. The use permit was issued on 29 September 1913.

The style is Art Nouveau, or Secession, shaped by Ödön Lechner's national style and by late Viennese Secession. The brick facade has a wrought-iron main gate flanked by two smaller entrances, coloured artificial stone decoration and a two-line Hebrew inscription from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17). Inside, according to the sources, there are women's galleries, a central reading platform and a carved ark, with Transylvanian motifs in the wood carving, Zsolnay porcelain inlays on the columns of the eastern wall and windows by Miksa Róth. It can seat over a thousand people.

During 1944 and 1945 the building lay within the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of its furnishings were destroyed, and the complex was restored after 1945. By the end of the twentieth century the main synagogue had deteriorated and become unsafe to use. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the building's west corner. The mikveh, or ritual bath, which operated here from 1928, reopened in 2004 after renovation.

Sources describe the synagogue today as the religious and cultural centre of Pest's Orthodox community. Hungarian Wikipedia says the main synagogue can be visited, but another source mentions renovation works and fundraising for repairs, so the position may have changed.
Good to know
This is an active Orthodox synagogue. Check access and visiting arrangements directly with the community and the official sources before you plan a visit.
One source gives the way here as metro line M2 to Astoria or M4 to Rákóczi tér, then a short walk to Kazinczy Street.
From the street, look for the Hebrew inscription along the top of the facade, a verse from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17).

historyIntro: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue was built in 1912 and 1913 for Pest's Orthodox Jewish community, after a design competition that the congregation decided against its jury. Its history runs through war damage, decline and a long search for a way to keep the community worshipping.

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia says the idea of an Orthodox synagogue in Erzsébetváros emerged in 1909, on a site on Kazinczy utca that belonged to the Pest Autonomous Orthodox Congregation. A design competition was announced on 25 June 1909. The jury chose the design of József Porgesz and Sándor Skultetzky, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and selected the design of the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. The detailed plans were approved on 8 November 1910.

The school and the community headquarters of the complex were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912. In July 1913, because of delays and unexpected costs, the Löffler brothers submitted a revised facade design, which Hungarian Wikipedia describes as plainer with lower material costs (English Wikipedia describes the change as more ornate). The official use permit was issued on 29 September 1913. A mikveh, or ritual bath, began operating in the building in 1928.

In 1944 and 1945 the building lay in the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of the furnishings was destroyed, and the complex was restored and the furnishings reconstructed after 1945. In the following decades the main synagogue deteriorated, and by the end of the twentieth century it was unheatable and unsafe. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the corner of the site by the engineer Sándor Bokor. The mikveh reopened in 2004 after renovation funded by private donations.

name: Újlak Synagogue — Frankel Leó Street
description: The Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, known earlier as the Újlak Synagogue, is a neo-Gothic brick synagogue consecrated in 1888 and later enclosed by a 1920s residential building. It is the home of an active Neolog congregation in Buda's 2nd district, and it appeared in the 1999 film The Taste of Sunshine.

children.text: The synagogue at Frankel Leó út 49 is in Újlak, in Budapest's 2nd district on the Buda side. Its present name is the Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, and Újlak Synagogue is its former name. It belongs to the Buda Jewish Community, follows the Neolog movement and the Ashkenazi prayer rite, and has Tamás Verő as its rabbi. The community's website, frankel.hu, publishes its weekly prayer times and contact details.

The foundation stone was laid in 1887, the building was completed in 1888 and it was consecrated on 8 August 1888. Sándor Fellner designed it in the neo-Gothic style, on the site of an earlier synagogue that was about a hundred years old. It originally stood free of other buildings, with its entrance on what was then Zsigmond utca, now Frankel Leó út, among single-storey houses, a kosher butcher shop and community apartments. It measures about 21.5 metres by 19 metres and was built for about 400 worshippers.

In the 1920s a residential building was constructed around the synagogue. It was handed over on 1 August 1928 and was designed by Dezső Jakab and his son-in-law Aladár Sós, on the initiative of a former community president, Berthold Beer. The synagogue itself was rebuilt at the same time, given reinforced concrete floor slabs and joined to the residential building, so that today it sits inside the block.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a three-bay facade of clinker brick with plaster detailing, stepped gables, pointed-arch windows and stone Tablets of the Law at the top. Inside are a wooden bimah, two seven-branched menorahs, an ark decorated with the Star of David and the Tablets of the Law, three women's galleries lit by pointed-arch windows and triple cross vaults. Marble plaques on the walls commemorate Holocaust victims and former chief rabbis.

At the end of the Second World War the synagogue was used as a stable, and the Jewish residents of the building were deported in 1944. A black marble plaque in the courtyard, unveiled in 2014, commemorates them. The residential building and the synagogue survived the siege of Budapest almost intact. The synagogue was used as a prayer house again under socialism and was completely renovated in 2000. It was also a filming location for Szabó István's 1999 film A napfény íze, The Taste of Sunshine.
Good to know
This is an active community synagogue inside a residential building. Use the contact details on frankel.hu to ask about access, and check prayer and service times there.
A memorial plaque for the residents deported in 1944 is in the courtyard, so ask the community before entering the building.
The synagogue is at Frankel Leó út 49 in Újlak, so it combines with a walk through that part of the 2nd district.

historyIntro: The Frankel Leó Street Synagogue was consecrated in 1888 as the Újlak Synagogue and was later enclosed by a residential building. It has served an active congregation through war, socialism and a renovation in 2000.

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records that the foundation stone was laid in 1887, the building was completed in 1888 and it was consecrated on 8 August 1888. Sándor Fellner designed it in the neo-Gothic style, and it replaced an earlier synagogue that was about a hundred years old. It was originally freestanding, with its entrance facing what was then Zsigmond utca, now Frankel Leó út. Single-storey houses, a kosher butcher shop and community apartments stood around it, and it was built for about 400 worshippers.

In the 1920s a residential building was constructed around the synagogue. It was handed over on 1 August 1928, designed by Dezső Jakab and his son-in-law Aladár Sós on the initiative of a former community president, Berthold Beer. At the same time the synagogue itself was rebuilt, with reinforced concrete floor slabs, and was joined to the residential building.

At the end of the Second World War the synagogue was used as a stable, and the Jewish residents of the building were deported in 1944. A black marble plaque in the courtyard, unveiled in 2014 for the seventieth anniversary, commemorates them. The residential building and the synagogue survived the siege of Budapest almost intact. Under socialism the synagogue functioned again as a prayer house, and in 2000 it was completely renovated. Today it belongs to the Buda Jewish Community, which follows the Ashkenazi prayer rite.

title: The Danube, at your pace
eyebrow: RIVERSIDE WALKS & A CITY SEEN FROM THE WATER
summary: Riverside walks, bridges and a city seen from the water.

heroImage.alt: The Chain Bridge lit up at night over the Danube with Buda Castle glowing behind
heroImage.creditTitle: Széchenyi Chain Bridge in Budapest at night.jpg

intro: The Danube is what holds Budapest together. Buda rises in hills on one bank and Pest spreads out flat on the other, and almost every classic view in the city is a view across the water. You can see the river from a bridge, a promenade, a hilltop terrace or a boat, and each gives you a different city.
highlights: Walk a stretch of either embankment before choosing a boat.
Check the exact departure pier and route for any cruise.
Evening departures vary with season and sunset.

children.text: Treat the riverfront as a route rather than a single stop. On the Pest side the embankment runs past the Chain Bridge, the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences towards the Parliament, and the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial sits on the same stretch. On the Buda side the road below Castle Hill starts at Clark Ádám Square, the foot of the Chain Bridge and the funicular.
Each bank is the viewpoint for the other. The Pest promenade looks up at Castle Hill and the Bastion; the terraces on Castle Hill look back across to the Parliament and the Pest skyline.
Pest bank: Chain Bridge → Gresham Palace → Shoes on the Danube Bank → Parliament.
Buda bank: Clark Ádám Square → the foot of Castle Hill → the Castle Garden Bazaar.
Leave time to stop: most of the good moments here are unplanned.

The Chain Bridge is the obvious first crossing, linking Széchenyi István Square in Pest with Clark Ádám Square in Buda. Walking it rather than riding over gives you time to look downstream and upstream, and the bridge ends make natural starting points for either side of the city.
If you have time for a second crossing, pick one further along the river and compare the angle: every bridge frames the Parliament, Castle Hill and Gellért Hill a little differently.

sections.title: See the city from the water

children.text: A river cruise changes the scale of the city and puts the Parliament and Castle Hill in one frame. Formats differ widely: shorter daytime sightseeing trips, evening cruises when the riverside landmarks are lit, and longer trips with dinner or drinks.

GoToBudapest does not take bookings. Compare the route, departure pier, duration and what is included directly with each operator, and check accessibility for your own needs. Our guide explains how to choose between daytime, evening and dinner formats.

sections.title: Take a green break on the river

children.text: Two places let you leave the pavements without leaving the water. Margaret Island is a green island in the middle of the Danube for walks and a slower pace, and Kopaszi-gát is a waterside green area on the Buda side.

Embankments are largely flat, but Castle Hill and Gellért Hill are steep, and surfaces can be uneven. Wind off the river can make evenings feel cooler than the forecast, so carry a layer outside summer. Opening times, boat departures and seasonal services change; confirm them with the operator before you travel.

faqs.question: Do I need a cruise ticket to enjoy the Danube?
faqs.answer: No. The public riverfront and bridges offer excellent views without booking a boat.

faqs.question: Are all cruises the same?
faqs.answer: No. Check the route, boarding pier, operating dates, inclusions and cancellation conditions for the specific departure.

placesIntro: Landmarks, memorials and green spaces on or beside the Danube, on both banks.

title: Soak up the city
summary: Build a slower day around a thermal-bath visit.

heroImage.alt: Bathers in the outdoor pools beneath the colonnades of the Széchenyi Thermal Bath

intro: Bathing is part of how Budapest rests. Some baths are grand historic complexes, some are small Ottoman-era-style Turkish baths, and others are open-air pools that only run in season. The best visit is the one that suits the rest of your day, so choose the bath around the neighbourhood you are already exploring.
highlights: Gellért Bath is closed for renovation.

sections.title: Pair a bath with a neighbourhood

children.text: Széchenyi Thermal Bath sits in City Park, so it fits naturally with a slow day around Heroes' Square and the park. On the Buda side, Rudas, Lukács and Veli Bej are close to the river and Gellért Hill, which makes them an easy follow-on to a morning on Castle Hill. Palatinus is on Margaret Island and works well after a walk on the island.
Thinking in neighbourhoods keeps travel time down and leaves the baths as the relaxed part of the day instead of an extra errand.

sections.title: Choose the kind of bath you want

children.text: Large thermal complexes combine several pools, steam and sauna areas. Turkish-style baths such as Rudas and Veli Bej offer a quieter, more traditional atmosphere, and both have sessions and access areas that vary by day and time, so check which one applies to your chosen date.
Open-air pools and beaches such as Palatinus, Lupa Beach and the Római Open-Air Bath are seasonal. Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a family-oriented water-park setting rather than a historic bath.

sections.title: Check the status before you plan

children.text: Gellért Thermal Bath is currently closed for renovation. The operator states that reopening is planned for 2028, which is not a confirmed date, so build your bath day around another venue. Seasonal baths can be closed outside their season and may change dates from year to year.

Bring swimwear and a towel unless the venue says it provides them, and check which facilities your ticket covers. Age rules, mixed or single-gender sessions, pool access and dress requirements differ between baths. GoToBudapest does not show ticket prices or availability, so confirm everything on the bath's own website.
Choose one bath rather than two: it is meant to be slow.
Check the day-specific session and access information.
Plan how you will get there and back before you get wet and tired.

faqs.question: Is Gellért Bath open?
faqs.answer: No. The operator reports a renovation closure with a planned reopening in 2028, which is not a confirmed date.

faqs.question: Are Budapest thermal baths suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Admission rules differ by venue and area. Check the operator's age restrictions before buying tickets.

placesIntro: Every bath in the directory, with seasonal and closure notices where they apply, plus two places that pair well with a bath day.
